newsitem.title: FRANCE: French leaders' ratings edge up in latest poll.
newsitem.headline: French leaders' ratings edge up in latest poll.

text.p: The approval ratings of French President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe are edging upwards but most voters remain unhappy with the way their country is governed, an opinion poll said on Tuesday.
The BVA poll for the weekly Paris Match found that, just 13 months ahead of general elections, only 21 percent of people aged 18 and over are satisfied with the centre-right government's performance.

While that is an improvement of three percentage points over a similar poll conducted a month earlier, two out of three nonetheless say they would back a no-confidence vote in parliament, a figure unchanged from the previous month.

"Despite these encouraging signs for the executive, the trends appear, from an electoral point of view, to be above all favourable to the (opposition) Socialist Party and its various allies on the left," BVA said in an accompanying analysis.

If elections were held today, the left would win 31.5 percent of the vote, an increase of two percentage points over the past month, to 36.5 percent for the majority, a decline of less than one percentage point, the pollsters said.

Surprisingly, support for the far-right National Front softened in the latest poll to 12 percent of the vote from 14 percent a month earlier despite a major victory for the party in a city hall election in southern Vitrolles.

The survey found that 27 percent of voters were happy with Juppe's performance while 53 percent were pleased with Chirac's handling of the presidency, an improvement for both men of one percentage point over the previous month.

Finally, the poll found that, in the event the funds became available, far more voters would prefer a cut in France's Value Added Tax than in the less burdensome tax on income, which the Juppe government cut for 1997.
It said that 62 favoured a reduction in VAT, 17 percent backed a cut in the income tax and 19 percent a cut in fuel taxes. The remaining two percent had no opinion.
The survey relied on interviews with 949 individuals conducted last Friday and Saturday.
